Mr. Chairman, I suppose this is the only item in the minister's estimates under which we will have the opportunity of discussing matters of a general character. With that in mind I should like to discuss the matter of the appointment of port surveyors. Owing to the changing of the Canada Shipping Act in its application to load lines, it became necessary to facilitate the operations of shipping, to appoint surveyors. Particularly was that so in those ports where lumber was the chief export. I suggest the port of Port Alberni has not been treated fairly.
Two men

and I understand they are capable men-have been appointed in Vancouver, and one in Victoria. The man in Victoria is authorized to carry out the supervision of ships loading lumber not only at Victoria but at points such as Nanaimo and Ladysmith. However the work in connection with the port of Alberni is being done by the man from Vancouver. I wish to emphasize that I have no complaint to make against the ability of that man. But the situation is such that shippers of lumber from the port of Port Alberni are operating under a very heavy handicap. In one sense that port is somewhat remote from Vancouver. That is to say a full day's time is required to get there, and another day to get back. The work is of such a character that a local man should be on hand to do it. It is not merely a matter of looking at a ship and saying, "All right, you can take the boat out." Constant
or at ltast intermittent supervision is required while the boat is being loaded, and that attention cannot be given by a man whose residence is a day's journey away.
The port of Port Alberni is deserving of careful consideration, because it is the third largest shipping port in the province of British Columbia. Hon. members may be surprised to learn that we out-rate Victoria, the capital city. We ship more lumber from the port of Port Alberni than is shipped from Victoria. Yet, when there is a man stationed at Vancouver we have not one at Port Alberni, with the result that there are several forms of injustice. The fee for inspecting a boat is ten dollars. I do not know who is supposed to pay it, but in the last analysis no doubt it is the shipper of the lumber. If the man has to come from a distance the shipper has to pay expenses both going and coming and living expenses. That, to begin with is an unfair charge, because it handicaps the shippers at Port Alberni who are in competition with other shippers.
Yet that is not the most important feature. This is a technical matter with which I am not thoroughly familiar; to decide where a load line shall be is an extremely complicated problem, under the new regulations. A man thoroughly versed in loading lumber, a marine man and one who has to have quite a good education, must do the work. The particular spot where the load line is to be placed is not so much his concern; that is ascertained by a preliminary surveyor. The chief duty of the port surveyor is to ascertain the amount of lumber that shall be put on the deck load. To those who do not understand marine matters I should explain that the surveyor could come along and say, " Well, take a thousand feet off that deck load." It would be easily done. However that is not the way it works out. A man may have a million and a half feet of lumber to ship. He knows where it is going. Some of it may be of a specific kind, or of a type most adapted to be shipped on the deck. Perhaps because it is too long, or for some other reason it cannot be put below deck. Under those circumstances the shipper would have half a million feet to place on the deck. After he has completed loading and placed the half million feet on the deck the surveyor, who has not been in attendance when the work was in progress, may come along and say, " You will have to take two hundred thousand feet off." In that way the order is broken. It means that not only will he have to take off two hundred thousand feet, but he will have to take the whole deck load off, take out a certain portion of the lumber
Supply-Marine

below deck and replace it with some* of the deck load which had to be taken off under the direction of the surveyor. The shipper must have the top load go on the ship somewhere, so he has to take the whole half million deck load off, then take some out of the hold and replace it.
That is only one illustration. I am trying to indicate the necessity of the surveyor being in the immediate vicinity, so that he may be called or consulted during the progress of the loading. He may come down and say, " That ship is sinking too fast by the head; I do not think I will allow any more in the forward hold"-or on the deck load, as the case may be. Under those circumstances the shipper guides himself accordingly, and makes appropriate arrangements. But when the surveyor is a day's journey away, he cannot give that supervision. He would not be paid if he came between times. These facts illustrate the necessity of always having a local man on hand. Of course he would not have to stand and watch the ship being loaded. The S10 would not be sufficient for him to do that, but he can glance at it from time to time.
Although I have discussed the most important feature, there is another one worthy of consideration. Very often 'the ships are running strictly on schedule time. If in loading they are detained more than a certain number of hours there are heavy demurrage charges. They do not know exactly when the boat will be completely loaded; possibly they cannot tell within forty-eight hours. If a surveyor is sent from Vancouver to be on hand at the time the shipper anticipates the boat will be loaded, and upon his arrival it is not loaded, there are all binds of trouble. If on the other hand when they send for him they find he has gone north of Powell River or some other comparatively remote port then the boat is tied up and someone has to bear heavy demurrage, perhaps $500 a day. For all these reasons and others which I could indicate I would impress upon the minister the necessity of appointing a local man, even if he is only an acting port inspector. Sudh men can be got at the port of Alberni, thoroughly competent to do the work. It is going to create a quite unnecessary handicap on this industry, which as we all know is struggling desperately at the present time. There are two or three mills that have been shut down most of the winter and they are just beginning work on a very meagre basis now, and should not be subject to any avoidable 'handicap. If I were asking the government to spend money it would be different,

but I am not; I am simply asking them to appoint a competent man in Port Albemi to do this work, as they have done in Vancouver. The Vancouver man is too far away, and the expense and time to bring him is too great. I do ask the minister to look very thoroughly into this phase of the situation. Perhaps he can give me some information now.
Carried.
No, it is not carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am
glad my hon. friend has brought this question before the committee. It is the first intimation I have had of any complaint about the surveyors we have on the Pacific coast for the enforcement of the load line convention. But the desire of the government is that our exporters and shippers shall have all possible facilities. I will be pleased to inquire, and if we can do what my hon. friend suggests, appoint a surveyor especially for the port of Albemi, we will do dt. I shall be happy to inquire.

I thank the minister. I might say that the government have a little interest in Port Alberni. They put a timber assembly wharf there that cost $125,000, and it has paid its way "from the grass roots," so to speak, the only wharf in Canada that has been known to do that. It is a credit to the foresight of the late ministry, so the government has some interest in seeing that it is made a success. I do not want the minister to take it that I have any complaint about the men appointed, they are quite competent men, the only thing is that it needs a local man.
While I am on my feet and before my hon. friends opposite cry "carried" again, I would ask the minister if he has any intention of building another lighthouse tender. These matters are just as important to the Pacific coast as the grain situation is to the prairies; we sat here very patiently while the Grain Act was being discussed, and we ask the same courtesy of hon. members now. I think I brought the question of a lighthouse tender to the attention of the minister last fall. The only boat doing the work now is the Newington; she is old and never was a very suitable boat. They had a very good boat some years ago but it had to be thrown aside. Some day that Newington is going to break down, it is far gone in a senile condition now, and when it does break down there is going to be a desperate situation in connection with the lighthouse service. Notwithstanding the need for economy, which I quite admit, I think it is poor policy not to foresee the more or less

Supply-Marine
immediate need for another boat. You cannot pick up suitable lighthouse tenders in a day or two, they have to be built. I hope the minister will give some assurance that even if he is not able to get one immediately he at least has it in his mind to arrange to build such a boat.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: As to the necessity of replacing that boat by a new one, I am quite in accord with my hon. friend. The reports of my officials are to the same effect. But this year we have to cut down expenditure, so unfortunately the project will have to be postponed until next year.

Just one word more. I am
glad to find myself so much in accord with the minister's views. I want to ask a question which is not of a critical character. I see in a local paper that a patrol cutter apparently called the Adversus is going to leave Halifax on May 5th to take up patrol work on the Pacific coast. Could the minister advise us as to the character of this boat and the work it will be engaged in, or what kind of boat it will replace? Is it intended to replace the Thiepval, or what is it intended to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am sorry I cannot
give a definite answer to my hon. friend, as this boat belongs to the preventive service of the customs department.
I observe the estimate does not provide for the salary of a chief engineer. Is it the intention of the department to do away with the services of the chief engineer?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
According to an order in council adopted some months ago, all
positions vacant at a certain date were abolished, automatically. But we have in the contingencies estimates sufficient money to provide for it when the appointment is made.

I notice on page 82 of the estimates there are quite a number of items in connection with the radio service. I find there is a director of radio service at 85,220; superintendent of radio service, $3,960; senior radio electrical engineer, $3,840; and chief radio inspector, $3,060; and senior radio inspectors, two, at $2,580; a total of over $21,000 for these officials in the radio branch. I thought it was understood that when the commission took over the service they would administer it. I would like to ask the minister if those positions I have referred to are independent of the commission, if those men will be retained in the service doing the same work as they w'ere doing before, and if the commission will carry on a different branch of the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Radio under the Department of Marine is quite separate from the radio commission. The radio commission attend to broadcasting; they may have their own engineers for broadcasting. The Marine department attends to communication and "trouble" services all over the country, and radio direction finding. So we have to retain our own engineers and staff.
Now that radio has been mentioned perhaps this is a favourable opportunity to refer to a matter that was brought up in the house some few days ago-

Has any progress been made regarding the appointment of a deputy minister of marine? How can the department get on without a deputy?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

Certainly; my
hon. friend has that privilege, but there is a particular item a little later on with regard to radio.

With further reference
*to the appointment of a deputy minister of marine, some time ago I directed a question in that regard to the minister, who referred me to the Prime Minister. I asked the same question of the Prime Minister, but I could not get a definite answer. Now the question has been asked again by the hon. member for Gaepe, and I should think the Minister of Marine and the Prime Minister have had time to consider the situation and decide what is to be done. Surely they are not going to leave that position vacant for another year. I think it is in the interests of the department, of the people in this country generally and also of the government that such a high post should be filled as quickly as possible. I am sure that in the department there are competent officials who might be promoted; other
Supply-M arine

persons have been mentioned with reference t-o this position as well, and I think it is necessary for the proper conduct of the affairs of the country that this appointment should be made. I have no doubt it would be a great help to the minister if he could be relieved of all the work of administration in connection with his own department, and he could do that by obtaining the services of a well qualified, well equipped man. Sometimes my hon. friend has to go away; for instance, last year he made a successful trip to Spain. Perhaps next year he may go to another country to represent Canada, perhaps Russia, and the department will be rudderless, operating without proper direction. I think we should have from the minister a statement as to the approximate date when this position will be filled.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I do not think it is
fair for my hon. friends to ask the minister when such an appointment will be made, when it is well known that under the law the appointment is made by the Prime Minister. I do not understand why the matter is brought up when the Prime Minister is not in his seat.

The other day the Prime Minister told me the matter was under consideration. Surely in the interval, and especially in view of the fact that we are getting towards the end of the session, some progress has been made in the matter. I know both my hon. friend and the Prime Minister are busy, but I would ask the hon. gentleman now whether an application or recommendation has been received with regard to certain persons in connection with this position. The .minister cannot make the country believe that the Prime Minister does the whole thing alone. We know he does most of the work of the government, but surely my hon. friend will not let anything be put over him; surely he will not lot the Prime Minister dictate to him how his own department shall be run. I do not think the hon. gentleman would let the Prime Minister appoint, without consultation, without advice and without authority, a man whom the minister himself might not trust and whom he might not care to have administering his department. It is very good to have the Prime Minister running the country and all the departments of the government, as we surmise he does, but I have known my hon. friend in a professional and business way, and from the way he has carried on his department and from the appointments he has made I am reasonably sure that he would not

allow the Prime Minister to force him to accept some person whom he might not like. I think the country should know when this position, which is one of the most important in the country, is to be filled. It has been vacant for almost a year now, but when we ask the minister when the appointment will be made we are told that the Prime Minister has the last say.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: That is the law.

But the Prime Minister is not in his seat. My hon. friend wants the country to believe that he is going to submit like a good little boy to the dictates of the Prime Minister. I do not believe it and the country will not believe it. We want to know when this position will be filled.
Carried.
I have put a direct question to the minister; I asked if he has received any applications for that position or if certain persons have been recommended to him. I should like an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Everyone knows that all applications must be directed to the Prime Minister, who appoints the heads of departments. I am surprised to hear my hon. friend say that he does not think the minister will let the Prime Minister go over his head in the making of this appointment. That is not the question at all; the law says that the heads of departments shall be appointed by the Prime Minister, and I believe in abiding by the law. I cannot tell my hon. friend when the appointment will be made; that question should be directed to the Prime Minister.
Then I will direct another question to the minister. Is it not a fact that applications for this position go to the minister, and has he received any application from any person?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, the applications go to the Prime Minister, who makes the appointment.
Then let me ask the minister if he has heard of any application being made for that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not attach much importance to gossip.
Has the minister himself received any application for that position?
The minister has already answered that question.

My hon. friend is not the minister. I should like an answer to my question, which I think is a fair one.

I think the question of this appointment has been a great disappointment to the country.

We were led to believe that the government intended to reduce all the estimates, but I notice an increase of $4,500 here. If the Department of Marine is carrying on all the services it carried on previously; if it has been found necessary to increase the estimates by $4,500 surely it follows that a deputy minister is needed. If there is no need for a deputy minister now surely there was no need for one in former years; t'he money paid previously must have been thrown away. I think it is up to the minister to give us a clear understanding of this matter. First he should tell us why the vote is increased by $4,500, and then he should say whether it is necessary to have a deputy minister and, if so, when that appointment will be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is mistaken; we have a total decrease of $9,054 in civil government. In the first item there is a decrease of $13,554, and there is an increase of $4,500 in the contingency item. As I said a moment ago, the position of chief engineer is not provided for in the first item, but it will be looked after under the next item. That might explain the increase of $4,500 in the second item, which is more than offset by a decrease of $13,554 in the first item.

Along with other members of the cabinet the minister represents the Montreal district. Has he taken cognizance of the resolutions passed yesterday by the chamber of commerce and the board of trade of Montreal, representing the business men of that city, to the effect that the government has made no attempt whatever to reduce the expenditures of this country? Is he prepared to apply the recommendations of those bodies to his own department?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have not yet taken communication of any resolution adopted by the chamber of commerce or the board of trade of Montreal, but I may inform my hon. friend that since we have been in office we have abolished over four thousand positions and reduced expenditures accordingly.
And increased unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I am sure that those who criticize the government are not aware of these facts.

The chief organ supporting the government in Montreal, the Montreal
Gazette, one of the best newspapers in the dominion, published yesterday and the day before editorials which I commend to the minister; he should take them into consideration. As regards these four thousand employees the hon. gentleman now mentions, I do not know what their political complexion is but I do know that in my own constituency every man who has been dismissed is a Liberal. Yesterday the Postmaster General dismissed Edward E.'Sweetman of Port Daniel Centre, a man who had been for a considerable number of years in the service, and a request to have him retained was made by the Lord Bishop of Quebec. The minister no doubt overlooks that. Of these four thousand how many were Liberals and how many Conservatives? Can the minister tell me that?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend refers to the Montreal Gazette and mentions an article in that newspaper with reference to the necessity for reduction in expenditures. May I in turn refer him to another newspaper, the Journal, and ask him to read yesterday morning's editorial, which furnishes a complete answer to the article in the Gazette.

The citizens of Montreal declare that they are prepared to carry their share of the burden; the business men of that city are ready to pay their taxes. But they want this government to give some evidence of economy. They point out that there are three or four departments which could easily be abolished. Here, for example, we have two departments which might be under the minister, the Department of Marine and the Department of Fisheries, and on top of that we have a duplication so far as radio is concerned; the minister is running one part of the radio organization while the radio commission sees to the other part of it. The minister will have a staff of his own and the radio commission their own staff.
By the way, in the matter of radio broadcasting, has the minister received complaints within the last week with regard to duplication of services? Has it been represented to him that one service is running into another, that some of the most important services from the United States, the Columbia station, for instance, are being neutralized by the multiplication of services in this country? Is he prepared to look into this matter? I know the minister is sincere, and he is a young man in public life, so that he wants to make good. Surely therefore he must realize the importance of the representation made by the business men of Montreal. These men want
Supply-Marine

to see some tangible evidence of economy on the part of the government. If I had time I could go over a list of departments that could easily be done away with or merged into other departments. That is what the Gazette is pointing out, and it is what these business men of Montreal wish to see brought about. They do not want the government to cut down by ten cents the pay of the labouring classes, charwomen and the like; they want the government to practise real economy. Take the Department of Railways for instance. That used to be one of the most important departments; to-day, if you ask the minister for information, all he says is, "I cannot give any information; I shall have to ask Montreal." So that Montreal is running the railways. Well, what is the use of that department? Why not take canals and put them under the Marine department? That is where the department could perform a useful service. Again, take the Health department, another one to which attention has been drawn. That deals only with animals, because the health of human beings is looked after by the provinces. Here we have a department that could easily be done away with; the services now performed by the Department of Health, so far as animals are concerned, could be done by the Department of the Interior or some other branch of government, perhaps the Department of Agriculture. And so on. I really think the minister should give some attention to the request made by the business men of Montreal, who after all carry a large share of the burden of this country, and who rightly insist that the government should show some practical evidence of their willingness to cut down the expenses of this country as far as possible. God knows we are governed enough; we have nine provincial governments, hundreds of municipal governments and county councils, and altogether we are governed to death. We have reached the crossroads, and if the offer from the United States does not result in a change in our commercial relations I do not know what will happen.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I can assure the committee that we are taking every possible means to curtail expenses. As a matter of fact a great number of items voted last year in my department, though they were reduced votes, have not been fully expended. We have tried to curb expenditures to the limit, and we are as much in sympathy with the taxpayers of the country as the former government was, indeed perhaps more. As regards the duplication of services in connection with

radio, I do not think my hon. friend clearly understands the situation.

I read the Journal last
night. That newspaper is highly regarded by the minister and it complains that one of the best services from the United States, the Columbia station, is completely neutralized by duplication on this side.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
is referring to wave length, but that has nothing to do with my department. Our system is the same as the system in England, where the British Broadcasting Corporation and the Post Office Department divide the services involved in radio broadcasting. There, the Post Office Department attends to the collection of radio licences and interference troubles, and in Canada tlhe Marine department collects the licence fees and carries on the interference service, while the radio commission attends to broadcasting, interference between stations, wave lengths and so on. I do not think there is any duplication in service.
I understand that the radio commission was appointed as a non-political organization. That promise however has gone by the board with the others.
Faded away like the rest.

I understood that the commission would control radio in Canada but now we have a dual organization, the minister in charge of one and the commission in charge of the other. When we ask him for information in regard to radio he replies in the same way as the Minister of Railways, "You must ask the commission." When we ask a question we are told that it cannot be answered and we are referred to the commission. Who is to speak in this house for the radio commission? Is it going to be independent and above parliament?
I am an old-timer; I am an old fashioned politician and I can remember the time When a member of parliament was somebody. He was the connecting link between the people and the government of the day and was not handicapped by commissions. He had the trust of the people and if he was a government supporter, he had the trust of the ministers of the crown. If something went wrong there was someone who could be blamed- that was the old style responsible government. To-day we have so many commissions that the ordinary elector is bewildered. Some of the older generation say to me: When you went to parliament in the old days it meant some-

Supply-Marine-Radio
thing but now you do not seem to be able to do anything for us when we write to you. We have the railway commission, the radio commission, the soldiers' commission, the pension commission, the civil service commission and other forces of that kind. Yesterday I asked a question of the Minister of Railways in connection with a contract for railway ties which had been awarded but I could not obtain any information. As far as matters pertaining to radio are concerned, we seem to be in the same position. We are also in the same position in connection with the civil service. I voted for the civil service commission in 1908 when the Hon. Sydney Fisher introduced his bill. At that time we felt that it was necessary that a commission should be appointed to handle the inside service but we had no idea of making this commission applicable to the outside service. The Postmaster General demonstrated that last year when he took post offices having a revenue of under $400 per year away from the civil service commission.
I do not know where all these commissions are going to lead us. At the present time it seems that this house comes here merely to vote money and nothing else. On the one side, we have the party in power remaining silent; on the other we have a party which says what it likes or what it is allowed to say, and then everything goes by. When we go back to our electors they ask all kinds of questions but we find we are helpless as far as giving information is concerned. We find we are up against the civil service commission, the soldiers' commission or something else of that kind. I have been urging a case before the pension board for the last eight or nine years. This is a widow whose only son was killed in action; the municipality has to look after her but I have been unable to get one dollar for the poor woman. People are beginning to wonder just what is the use of having members of parliament when everything is being done by commissions made up of civil servants.
We all know how the different ministers are harrassed by office seekers. This has been the case ever since 1867 when this country was organized. A man who has served his party feels that he can come here and exact payment fer his services. They feel that when they work for a party and that party is in power, they should be rewarded. The country is spending thousands and even millions of dollars in keeping up these commissions. I understand two or three of these commissions are to be abolished by the amendment to the 53719-262
Pension Act introduced yesterday. This costly system of government is crushing the people of Canada. They are carrying a burden which we never had to carry in days gone by. I think the Montreal Gazette and the Montreal chamber of commerce are quite right in asking this government to make a determined effort to cut down the cost of government.

The hon. member for Bonaventure has referred to the article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette. There was also one which appeared in the Ottawa Journal, and I should like to ask the minister just which article is correct. No answer 1 That is your condemnation.

speechtext: A full discussion has taken place upon these two items.

When these items were up before a somewhat lengthy debate took place in connection with a new licence which had been issued by the department apparently in the absence of the minister. At that time I referred to complaints which had been brought to my attention as to the use being made of this station. The propaganda from this station was not against any political party or any municipality or province, it referred more particularly to the institutions of this country. It will be recalled that a
short time ago the minister, in reply to a question of mine, made a statement to the house with reference to the banning of Judge Rutherford's lectures from the radio. I do not know that I should have spoken at this time or dealt with the matter further had it not been that I assumed some responsibility for circulating throughout the country the answer made by the minister. I did this because I had received a good many communications protesting against the banning of those lectures, and I was not in a position to make any effective reply from my own knowledge. So that there may be no misunderstanding on the part of anybody, may I say that I am not at all in sympathy with Judge Rutherford's exposition of the scriptures. However to forbid men interpreting the scriptures and teaching whatever doctrines they see fit, so long as it is done without transcending the bounds of decency and without needless offence, does not agree with my views regarding religious liberty. Whether Judge Rutherford did or did not transcend those bounds I will not undertake to say. It seems however that the chairman of the commission objected that the judge in question had referred to him as a liar, a thief, a Judas and a polecat and therefore fit only to associate with the clergy. I agree that these are not complimentary remarks coming from any person.
It would seem however that Judge Rutherford has no monopoly on that kind of language. After I brought the matter up in the house I was waited upon by one of Judge Rutherford's disciples who protested against the reply which had been made by the minister. He called my attention to the fact that as long ago as August 16, 1927, there appeared in the Saturday Night, of which Mr. Charles-worth was the editor, an article dealing with Judge Rutherford and his propaganda. The article would indicate that when Mr. Charles-worth was placed in the position he now occupies, namely that of chairman of the 53719-262 J
radio commission, he was not entirely unprejudiced. Therefore in fairness I believe I should read some extracts from the article to ^how that Judge Rutherford had not a monopoly of offensive language. I have not time to read the whole of it, so I shall read only some extracts. The first is as follows:
Recently Toronto had the doubtful honour of entertaining once more a heavy-jowled flannel-mouth known as "Judge" J. F. Rutherford, grand vizier of the "Russellites" or the International Bible Students' Association, together with some thousands of his followers. What the said Rutherford is a judge of we do not know

perhaps of cigars, perhaps of fat swine -perhaps he is called judge by way of persiflage, just as an elevator man is called "Cap."
Then, further on:
The war is over and peaee loving people are willing to let by-gones be by-gones, but they do object to wandering blatherskites and professional liars starting the war all over again on Canadian soil. That Rutherford is a lying demagogue is apparent from the text of his addresses, in which he exploits the old fallacy that there is one law for the rich and another for the poor.
Towards the end of the article this complaint is made :
On the night of July 21, reputable fathers of families anxious to listen in on the progress of the Dempsey-Sharkey prize fight were kept out by the high power oratory at the Toronto Coliseum.
Mr. Chairman, I do not purpose to judge as between these two. I repeat however that the action of the radio commission is not in harmony with my views in regard to the rights of a man to promulgate whatever doctrines he wishes, providing he does so without undue offence. As I said, it is only because I assumed responsibility for sending out to some of my constituents the statement made by the minister, thinking that perhaps he had made a satisfactory answer to the question, that I feel somewhat under obligation to present the other point of view. Having done that I shall only further emphasize that Mr. Charles-worth apparently was not altogether unprejudiced when in his official capacity he dealt with Judge Rutherford.
Have you anything to show that the article was written by Mr. Charlesworth; is it over his name?
It appeared in the Saturday Night, a paper controlled by him.

No; he just
happened to be editor at that time. Is there anything to show that Mr. Charlesworth wrote the article? Let us be just to him.

It will 'be interesting to Tead what the Minister of Marine of that day had to say about the broadcasting activities of the International Bible Students; he cut them off.

This is not a matter between [DOT]one government and another. I have made my statement simply to satisfy people in my own constituency who have been exercised over the question as to whether or not the lectures should have been banned from the radio.

This matter is in the minds of a great many people in Canada to-day. At the outset let me say I have no brief for Judge Rutherford's organization, as I still adhere to that religious body known as the Presbyterians, .-and am content to hold to the eternal truths. No doubt many hon. members received communications regarding this matter. On behalf of the people who communicated with me I took the trouble to write Mr. Charlesworth. On March 27 last he replied to my letter stating, as the minister stated in the house, that Judge Rutherford had said he was a thief, a liar, a Judas and a polecat, and therefore fit to associate only with the clergy. Mr. Charlesworth further states:
{Mr. Macdougall.]
Ton will plainly see that a man who interlards such attacks with his interpretations of prophecy is an objectionable person to have on the air in Canada.
After that letter I began to answer all the communications that had been sent me, upon which occasions I quoted the remarks of Mr. Charlesworth. One of the people to whom I wrote took the trouble to communicate with Judge Rutherford, with the result that I received a letter from him only a few days ago. I believe it should be read to the house, because it deals with the allegations contained in Mr. Charlesworth's letter. The date of the letter is April 15 of this year:
Hon. T. Reid,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir,-
A letter just received by me quotes from a letter written by you on March 28th to Mr. A. Kennett of Vancouver, B.C., the following:
"Mr. Charlesworth makes the further statement that Judge Rutherford in his recent address called him a thief, a liar, a Judas and a polecat, and therefore, he stated, fit only to associate with the clergy."
Permit me to say, my dear sir, that never at any time in a public address have I even mentioned the name of Mr. Charlesworth and at no time have I ever indulged in such language as above quoted. Surely I should not be held responsible for what others may say. I have never yet applied such epithets to any public man.
I think in view of that reply from Judge Rutherford the minister should bring down the correspondence, especially the letters received by Mr. Charlesworth, if he did receive them, in connection with the statements made by Judge Rutherford. I think this matter should be cleaned up, because it is exercising the minds of many of our Canadian citizens, whether they agree with the judge's organization or not.

It has been . suggested that this is a partisan matter. As one who criticized the late government with regard to a similar ruling, I think I am clear of any charge of that kind. Further than that, I have no sympathy with the teachings of Judge Rutherford and his school. At the same time I do thank that we are facing here a serious situation. It seems to me that in this country in the past we have largely taken the view that religion was a private matter and that each man was free not only to hold his own religious beliefs but to give utterance to those beliefs, so long as he did not interfere with other people. If his beliefs differ from those of others I suppose he should be free to criticize the beliefs of others. That has always been the practice under

British law-that is so long as the criticism is not made in an offensive way. Someone near me suggests that parliamentary language should be used; I hope that it will be better than we have sometimes heard in this house!
As far as -the newspapers are concerned a great deal of latitude has been allowed in such matters. Some years ago the Orange Sentinel used to come to me free; I think there was a great deal of latitude permitted to the Orange Sentinel. On one or two occasions I have lived in a house to which Roman Catholic papers came, I think they were allowed a very considerable degree of freedom in criticizing people of other denominations. Sometimes these various religious bodies crossed the line of decorum in criticizing others, but this was generally permitted so long as they did not cause trouble in the community.
Now we have a new medium of communication, the radio, and it would seem that there should be very great care exercised here. I can understand that with this medium of communication, being much more powerful than that of the press, there may be possibly even greater dangers and hence greater care should be exercised. We have now not merely a certain control by the government of radio, but we have gone further, we have made radio a public utility and have placed in charge of it a commission that is almost independent of parliamentary control. At the beginning of this new arrangement it seems to me highly desirable that we should place matters on a sound basis, or undoubtedly there is disaster ahead. About the only argument that I noticed the minister made the other day as he presented the case for the commissioners was that since Judge Rutherford lives outside of Canada he could not very readily come under our libel laws. There may be something to be said for that, but surely we should have some conclusive evidence, much more conclusive than has been furnished, that distinctly libellous utterances have been made, before action of this kind should be taken. I think there ought to be something in the nature of a trial before a man should be cut off. It ought not to be simply on the general principle that he lives outside of the country and is opposed to certain individuals or institutions in this country, that is too dangerous a position to take. I think we ought to have this cleared up, as has been suggested by the hon. member for New Westminster, by having the correspondence placed before us. If we once set this country by the ears over religious controversy we cannot tell where the matter
may end. I found an interesting sequel to this the other day in the Montreal Daily Herald of April 14, under the heading:
Recorder Flays Bible Students
Declares group guilty of publishing illegal literature Radio Commission
The article reads:
Tracts prepared and distributed by the International Bible Students' Association, although sprinkled with quotations from the prophets for authority, were found illegal by Recorder Gr. H. Semple yesterday, and Edward Noreworthy, a Montreal member of the association, was held responsible for them by the court. Sentence will be passed on April 21.
According to Recorder Semple's decision, the tracts, which constituted an invective against the Canadian radio commission for its ruling against J. F. Rutherford, ex-judge from Brooklyn and president of the association of uncensored radio speeches, were subversive in nature.
And here is given a quotation from the recorder's judgment:
The circular itself is but a protest-thinly veiled and replete with quotation from the prophets-against authority as constituted by the Radio Broadcasting Act. That is its preconceived, determined, and sole purpose; and in that respect it is subversive of peace, order, and good government.
The article concludes:
In the circular there was asked the question: "Have the people of Canada reached such a state of low intellectuality that they need to have a "wise" radio commission to approve what they shall hear about the Bible?
Now it seems to me that that is a most extraordinary decision. I am not suggesting that the minister or the radio commission are to be held in any sense responsible for the decision of Recorder Semple-

What decision is
that?
I have just read it.
It is not a decision of the minister or of this government. Some irresponsible-

Recorder Semple
is not irresponsible.

Well it does not
matter, you cannot attribute that to the minister or this government.

When I was interrupted I was in the midst of saying that I did not hold the minister or the commission responsible for the decision of Recorder Semple, but I do say that the fact that such a decision can be given seems to me to emphasize the necessity for much more care-

ful consideration of a matter of this kind. If we grant powers to a commission, and if when anyone chooses to protest against the decision of the commissioner his action is declared to be illegal, it seems to me that we have reached an intolerable situation. I cannot understand how there is any legal basis for this decision; however there it is, it shows what might happen if we allow this kind of thing to go on unchecked.
Curiously enough, in the Herald on the same page in another column over from this there is another item with regard to radio:
C. C. F. Flayed in Radio Talk by Gerald Almond
N. D. G. Candidate Calls Federation Necessary Evil of Centuries
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is the necessary evil of centuries, and it is "flayed" the very word used at the head of the other paragraph. Apparently it is illegal for Judge Rutherford to use invective against certain people or certain beliefs, but apparently it is quite proper for Gerald Almond, whoever he may be, to flay the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I suggest that we are going to have a great deal of trouble with the national radio commission if there is to be discrimination of that character. I can quite conceive that it may be necessary for the radio commission to establish some definite rules that certain personalities may not be permitted over the air. I would hope that the time has not come when they would insist that the policies of other churches, other political parties or other groups might not be criticized, since that would be an infringement on the right of free speech. I submit that there must not be discrimination of this character, and I think at least the minister should tell us to-day what principles are applied by the commission in deciding what is proper to be broadcast and what is not proper. That is what I should like to have from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I have not very much to say in reply to the remarks of my hon. friend. I have nothing to say with regard to the judgment rendered by Recorder Semple of Montreal; I do not think it is up to the minister or the government to criticize or pass judgment on a decision rendered by a recorder in Montreal or any other city in the country. If the matter should be brought up in a proper way and studied by the government perhaps we might have something to say, but at this moment I have nothing to add. With regard to the other question, the radio commission was organized under a statute unanimously passed by this house last

session, and they were given certain powers and a certain control over the radio stations in Canada. We have made the best possible appointments to that commission in order that the statute may be carried out properly. I am not prepared to say on what principles they base their decisions with regard to programs being broadcast from certain stations, but I have no doubt these commissioners will do their duty to the full and will maintain a proper control over radio stations. I suppose they must decide whether or not to prohibit utterances which may be made against good government, against the institutions of the country or against public feelings throughout Canada, but I am not prepared to say what their principles are. At the present time they are the sole judges, with full control over the radio stations.

I have not asked
the minister to defend or criticize the decision of Recorder Semple, but I do say that when we have a man awaiting sentence for having published a tract which has been held to be illegal simply because it criticizes the radio commission we have a serious situation. Here we have a roundabout way of making a law. A man is to be sentenced for having criticized a ruling made by the commissioners. Surely this parliament has the supreme law making power in the country, we have some right to say what the law shall be. It is absurd if we cannot get from the minister to-day what are the criteria used by the commission. Surely there must be some fundamental principles adopted by the commission which would be general in their character. I can quite understand that the commissioners must be given a good deal of latitude and discretion in handling this business, but I think we should know the general principles under which they operate, especially when a ruling may lead to a situation such as the one to which I have referred.

I wonder if the minister is
prepared to give the committee the details of where Judge Rutherford made this statement and to whom and when it was made, because, as I say, this matter has been exercising the minds of many people all over the country. This man says that he never made the statement at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: What statement?

The statement accredited to
him by Mr. Charleswonth, who said that in his recent fulminations Judge Rutherford called him a thief, a liar, a Judas and a polecat. Judge Rutherford says he made no such utterances. In view of the fact that this

question is arousing considerable discussion all over the country I think we should be told when Judge Rutherford made that statement, where he made -it and to whom he made it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The statement I gave the other day emanated from the radio commission, as I stated quite plainly. I thought those words were taken from the letter which was circulated all oveT Canada, though I am not sure. I do not remember whether or not those exact words were contained in that letter.
The letter from whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Presumably from
Judge Rutherford. The letter and signature were printed and a copy was left at every door, according to my information; I know I received a copy at my office here and also ait my house in Montreal.

Turning away from the subject which 'has interested the committee for some time, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to a matter which I brought up in the house last year and again during the present session. I refer to the situation with regard to the radio station known as CKOK at Windsor. When I referred to this matter previously I said that I had received information to the effect that this station was owned and controlled by United States capital, that the programs came almost entirely from the United States, and that the advertising took up more than the percentage of time allotted by the rules of the commission. At that time the minister made the statement that he was not quite satisfied with the way that station was conducted. Since then I have heard that this station has been combined with the station operated at London, I think by the London Free Press, and I have heard also that 'the Windsor station has been granted an. increase in power. I rise to-day merely to ask the minister whether he can give any further details with regard to these points.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Before the beginning
of the fiscal year I received a recommendation from the radio commission authorizing the amalgamation of the London station with the Windsor station, with an increase in power to 5,000 watts.
To both stations?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I think the London
station will disappear, and the Windsor station will have 5,000 watts power. They intend to conduct a very powerful station, and I know the radio commission is looking after the programs.
What have they ascertained?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My information is
that 'they propose to maintain studios both in London and in Windsor, and I am told that this will be a great improvement.

With all due respect to the minister I am afraid he has not given the committee a great deal of information; the only thing he has told us is that these two stations have been amalgamated. It does occur to me that if this station is to serve western Ontario, to select Windsor, which is the extreme western boundary, is not so wise as to have London. I am not an expert in radio matters but I am wondering why they should establish a station or continue a station at the extreme edge of the country rather than in central Ontario, thus reaching what is usually known as the western peninsula of the province. I wish the minister would say something in that regard. He has given no information whatever as to whether the station is now completely under Canadian control, unless he regards the fact that it has been amalgamated with the London station as proof that it is now Canadian. Further, with regard to programs, I believe that what 'he assures the committee is that in future they will be largely Canadian, but I am afraid there has not been much progress in that regard, nor has anything been done in the matter of the percentage of advertising, which under the rules of the commission is limited to five per cent of the time of any program. With regard to the increase of power, he states that Windsor station is to have 5,000 watts. I understood that they had 5,000 watts before, and if that is so there is no increase there. It is interesting to note that the London station is to be abolished, but I would point out that the other station is not nearly so well located as the ordinary layman would think for the proper distribution of radio programs.

As regards the Essex Broadcasting Company, fifty-one per cent of the stock is owned by Canadians, and there are options and agreements in escrow by which they can exercise very shortly the right to own and control two-thirds of it. The Essex broadcasting station is one of the most up to date stations in the world. There is nothing on the North American continent that can beat it. It was built at a cost of S150.000 and the annual expenditure is something like $115,300. The studio in Detroit is used in conjunction with it but the main station is in Windsor and there are a greater number of employees there than on the other side, where advertising from American sources is secured.

I have never been able to hear the London station in Windsor; it has only a small radius whereas the station in Windsor will almost reach the North Pole. When they were canvassing for advertising they could not get a great deal from Canadians, but after the time had been allotted to American advertising the Canadians were regretting that they had not taken advantage of the opportunity that had been offered them. When the new contracts are made out however the greater part of the advertising will be Canadian.
Referring to Judge Rutherford, I wish the hon. member for New Westminster had listened in last Sunday afternoon to what the so-called judge had to say. As a rule I do not listen to nuts over the radio, and I think this man has been getting too much free advertising, especially in this country. I have received numerous letters with regard to Judge Rutherford and I do not hesitate in any of my replies to say just what I think of him. It seems to me a disgrace and almost a crime that he should have got off the stuff he did last Sunday; it was most unfortunate that what he said should have been heard in any Christian home in this country. What he had to say about Christian ministers was almost a crime.
And the Liberals defend him in this house to-day.

Ever since I heard the hon. member for Richelieu express himself in regard to Judge Rutherford three or four years ago I have been interested in the man's career and I do not think he has improved one bit. I do not know how it was that his broadcast reached Walkerville last Sunday.
What station was he broadcasting from?

Neither Columbia nor CKOK. A good deal of complaint about CKOK came from one of the stations in Detroit. They happened to put over wrong information and when the mistake was discovered they regretted having brought the matter up.

Can the hon. member tell the committee why Windsor was selected instead of London for this station? Was it not because forty-nine per cent of the stock is owned in Detroit that the station was located in Windsor rather than in London?

The reason is that the London station has to be rebuilt. It has only a small radius, I do not know how many watts. In Windsor, however, there is a station 
that will reach almost any point on the continent.

Will my hon. friend tell me when the change of ownership took place? Not long ago I had undeniable evidence that the majority of the stock was owned in the United States and CKOK at Windsor was described as a Columbia basic station. When did the majority of the stock come to Canada? Is the hon. member quite certain it is a real bona fide transfer of stock and that the station is not really an American station using a Canadian channel?
I do not know the details, but I do know that it was the intention that the majority of the stock should be owned in Canada.

I can assure my hon. friend opposite that in the statements I made I was in no way supporting Judge Rutherford; I said so at the outset. As a matter of fact, in the letter I sent out to the people who had written to me on the subject I stated that if Judge Rutherford had made the statements attributed to him he should be shut off; I said I believed that no sensible man would make such statements. When I brought the matter up to-day the question at issue was this: Did he or did he not make those statements? It was said-Mr. Charlesworth told me-that Judge Rutherford had made these statements about him, but Judge Rutherford declared that never at any time had he made any such statements about any man. I have made my position quite clear, and yet the hon. gentleman gets up and says that we on this side are supporting the International Bible Students. I can tell him that when I listen in, if I do not like the program that is coming over I turn it off, and everyone else is at liberty to do the same. I have not yet received a clear statement from the minister in this matter and in courtesy to Judge Rutherford I am withholding my reply to him until I do. There are thousands of Canadians who are interested in what Judge Rutherford says, whether the rest of us believe in him or not.

I do not know why so much time is taken up discussing Judge Rutherford. If he did not make the particular statements to which reference has been made to-day, I know at any rate that he made other statements in the exhibition grounds in Toronto, which is in my riding, statements that incensed the whole city. He condemned the institutions of Canada, the United States and

Supply-M arine-Radio
Great Britain, and he condemned every other church but his own. Toronto does not want to hear him again over the radio.

We do not seem to
appreciate the fact that in this discussion a principle is involved. Down through the centuries there have been two ideas in conflict. One party has held that where anything occurs that looks like heresy, where any views are advanced that are contrary to the accepted opinions of the day, they should be put down by force. The other school holds that truth will ultimately prevail and that less harm is likely to be done by allowing the free expression of opinion than by any attempt to shut off opinions by force. I have no hesitation in saying that I belong to the school that believes in allowing a man to give free expression to his beliefs. I believe that ultimately truth will prevail and that if the views expressed are not in harmony with truth, they will run their course and ultimately disappear. I admit that the radio has introduced a more difficult problem than is entailed in the freedom of the pulpit or of the press and I confess it is hard to arrive at a final conclusion upon the matter. I think the radio commission would be well advised to hesitate before preventing people from preaching the doctrines in which they believe or interpreting the scripture in their own particular way. Less harm is likely to be caused by allowing freedom in this direction than by imposing restrictions. I realize the difficulties to be faced and that it takes a man of more than ordinary wisdom to arrive at a wise conclusion.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot possibly understand the minister's attitude. Just a few days ago we were considering the estimates of the Trade and Commerce department and an item came up for the administration of the Grain Act by the board of Grain commissioners. Members of this house have always had the privilege of discussing the expenditures of this commission. The money must be voted by parliament, and when the Minister of Trade and Commerce has had his estimates up for discussion he has had an officer of the board of grain commissioners sitting in front of him to give information. That has always been the practice. In every other instance when a commission is administering some utility for this dominion, the minister when his estimates are before parliament has an officer of the commission sitting in front of him because that is the only time hon. members on both sides of the house have the right to get the information they desire. In this instance I think it is doubly necessary. The radio commission has not by any means given even half satisfaction to the people of Canada. The complaints are very, very numerous. The case which was mentioned by my hon. friend from North Waterloo and by other members of the house is far from satisfactory to the people of that portion of Canada who think that the United States
Supply-M arine-Radio

have put it over our eye in the matter of the division of wave lengths. The Windsor station was started by a group of Americans, and it was started at Windsor, near Detroit, for one purpose, and that was to get in on a Canadian wave length, and by advertising sell American products through Michigan and Ohio and neighbouring states. That was the purpose. Fifty-one per cent of the stock in the station may be in the hands of Canadians; I shall not deny the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Robinson) to that effect. I have a very strong suspicion however that the men who hold forty-nine per cent of the stock control the policy of the station. I agree fully with the hon. member for North Waterloo that if a station is needed for western Ontario, it would be more properly located at a central point such as London, Stratford or Guelph. If eventually the national commission is to buy out and operate broadcasting stations I do not think the minister should allow the station in the city of London to be closed, and a high powered station in Windsor to be erected. I believe London is the place where the good station should be placed.
I mention these points to the minister for one reason: The people in Canada are wondering what is going to happen to the million dollars that is being voted. My own feeling is that the minister himself, with the brilliant departmental officers in his department, could have handled the whole matter during the period of depression very much better than any other body which could be set up. At the present time wa have the anomaly of the commission trying to develop Canadian programs, and giving licences to stations right on the American border. The minister knows very well that he has control of licences; he has said so. The commission has to control the stations, but the minister has to issue the licences. Therefore the minister must explain tc his followers in the house and to hon. members in the opposition why certain stations are placed at certain points. I submit to the minister that in connection with a matter as important as this, namely the location of a powerful station at a point far removed from the centre of the province, he should have a lot better answer to the question of the hon. member for North Waterloo than he has made. In regard to the question asked by the hon. member for South Perth, the minister should be able to get all the details from the officer of his department who is sitting in front of his desk.

The statement was made that I had not objected to the appointment of the radio commission. If I did not

do so, it was because I still had faith in the declaration of the Prime Minister that the radio commission would be a non-political organization. But when I saw the chief organizer of the Tory party in the province of Quebec made a member of the commission, that settled the matter, so far as I was concerned.

The board of grain commissioners have to secure a vote of money in this house. Their receipts and revenues are available to hon. members from the west who pay inspection fees. Eventually this radio commission will have substantial revenues. The minister should soon be able to tell us what stations are owned by the commission, the revenues from them, and what moneys are expended, so that the people of Canada may have some knowledge of what radio broadcasting is costing.
Personally I never have been in favour of the national broadcasting commission. I do not object to it however, and if it is well run it may be well worth while. But if we are to have a commission in control we expect to know what the revenues from the stations will be. We want to know something of the future plans. We do not want to vote millions of dollars for services, if those services are not to be an improvement or produce revenue. We have taken over the Canadian National Railways stations. How much of the million dollars is to be used for that purpose? Can the minister tell us that, or is the transaction to be merely a bookkeeping entry between two departments of government? I submit that the suggestion by the hon. member for South Perth is justified, namely that we should postpone consideration of this item until such time as the minister has more information.
I move we do that.

Mr. Chairman, I wish
to set out the viewpoint held by the people in northern Ontario. When the announcement was made in the House of Commons by the Prime Minister that radio broadcasting was to be under government supervision, so that greater service would be given to a greater number of people, his statement was well received in northern Ontario. In fact, in the first year we did not complain when radio licences were doubled in price, because we hoped then-and we still hope-that we would receive the service we deserve.
At the outset let me say that in our section of the country we believe the officials in the department have done good work. I make the statement sincerely, believing that they deserve praise. They sent men to my home town of Cochrane and to the town of Timmins

Supply-.M arine-Radio
who accomplished some of the work that our section of the country expected would be done. The fact remains however that after nearly two years of government supervision, radio programs in our section are in most cases from American stations; we receive practically no Canadian programs. Generally speaking we do not object to listening to the American stations; some of them are entertaining, and we are very glad to have them. We cannot lose sight of the fact however that we are part and parcel of Canada, and we are as much entitled to radio reception of Canadian programs as are the people in Ottawa, Toronto, Halifax or Montreal. I maintain that under present conditions unless we have a station built in our section of the country it will be impossible for us to receive radio programs from Canadian stations. We are not parochial in our views in this connection; it is not a matter of one locality having a station, and another not having it. Our object is to have a distributing station in northern Ontario which will benefit the whole of our population. All the territory west of North Bay and extending as far as Sioux Lookout and the Manitoba border W'ould be affected. It is possible to have a station on the height of land in the Porcupine district under which circumstances good reception would be assured to the people in the northern section of the province.
How far the government has gone in the matter I do not know. I do know, however, that the minister has received several petitions, and the commission has been informed as to conditions in northern Ontario. I will say further that the commission and the minister have sent very favourable letters to people in my constituency. Up to date, however, that is as far as they have gone. We are practical and logical, and realize that this problem cannot be solved in a day. The matter has 'to be thoroughly studied, and the Questions concerning the location of the station and the extension of services have to be given careful thought. There is a suggestion-from the Northern Tribune of Kapus-kasing-that a station be built on the James bay slope, taking in that section of the north country extending to the Hudson bay region to the north and the United States border to the south. I believe, however, that the location of the station should be left to the decision of the commission, after a thorough study of the situation. On the other hand, the people of Porcupine district state that the logical place for such a station is between Sudbury and Timmins. Then, that section of the country so well represented by the Minister of Mines maintain that it should
be on the height of land in the vicinity of Haileybury. However, these are mere matters of detail.
After careful consideration and analysis the commission will have to decide upon the point which would be most satisfactory to all sections of the population. They will have to visit northern Ontario in an official capacity; they will have to send their experts to find for themselves where the best results will be obtained. Those men will quickly realize that it is not a parochial question, and that the whole of the population in northern Ontario would be in agreement. We mean by that, that so long as 'the commission finds it possible to build a station which would be Strong enough and located at a point to give the best service to all the people, we will be satisfied.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that my plea is a very practical one. In our section of the country we only get the Canadian newspapers twenty-four hours after they are printed. Speaking of radio reception I will say that in the daytime we get practically only American programs; we rarely get a Canadian station. Sometimes we get Toronto but seldom do we get it fully. These facts alone should cause this house to realize that although we have a great number of radio owners in our section-it may be a revelation to this house that a very great number of settlers have radio sets, helping to make life a little brighter in the rural and colonization sections-the service they are getting is not satisfactory. I want to be practical; I am not going to criticize the commission, because I do not think they have yet had time to remedy the situation entirely. They have doubled the radio licence fee, which we gladly pay, but we think it is time that something tangible was done to show the people that the commission is alive to the situation existing in our section. I could quote at great length letters and petitions sent to the minister and the commission as to the anomalies that exist. This criticism is going to gather strength if during this summer some move is not made for the location of a good station that will give service to our section. I believe the minister is fully seized of the situation, and that the chairman and the commission also realize what we are up against. Public ownership of this great utility should be applied on a national scale, no section of the country should be neglected. Even if the department had to spend some money in our section that they have not to spend in the older sections I believe it is fully warranted, and cannot be done too soon. The sooner
Supply-M arine-Radio

it is made possible for radio owners to have access to Canadian programs, musical or otherwise, the better it will be for this nation. I repeat that in our section we have no great objection to hearing some of the wonderful programs that come from the south, but I believe that first of all we should have access to Canadian programs.
In order that the minister may fully understand the matter I am going to read an editorial from the Porcupine Advance which I believe puts the question very logically and in a very straightforward way. This article was published February 9 of this year. It is as follows:
Does the United States Rule the Waves?
Elsewhere in this issue wall be found a letter from an ardent radio fan. This letter voices the feelings of large numbers of radio owners in this section of Ontario. There are few areas where there are as many radio owners in proportion to population as in this north land, and it does not appear unreasonable to suggest that the large group of radio enthusiasts in this part of the country are entitled to more consideration than they seem to have received to date. After suffering for years with growing discouragement, radio fans in this district fed themselves with new hope when they read announcements to the effect that the new Canadian radio commission -was arranging a series of all-Canadian programs that would be a change, a relief and a joy to those who listen in up in this north land. After the surfeit of cheap jazz, sad southern humour, claptrap advertising and highly Americanized public addresses, programs of music promised to revive interest in the radio. Canada has artists of international fame. To have the Toronto symphony orchestra, the Vancouver symphony orchestra, the Grenadier Guards band, the Ritz Carlton orchestra, the Forty-eighth Highlanders band, the C. I. L. opera of the air, the Mendelssohn choir, the Hart House quartette, Edward Johnson, one of the world's greatest tenors, Dr. Frieker, deservedly famous as an organist-to mention a few only at random

this surely would cheer the heart of any lover of music owning a radio. Yet the first of the Canadian radio commission's special programs sunk all radio owners in deeper gloom than before,

because the program could not be heard at all in this part of the north.
That just corroborates the statement I made a moment ago, as far as our section of the country is concerned.
As the letter elsewhere in this issue explains, little else could be fairly expected. United States and Mexican stations are so powerful that Canadian stations have no chance at all. What seems to be needed first and foremost is at least one Canadian station with power enough to drown out, if necessary, the United States and Mexican stations that now monopolize the air. Some time ago it was suggested that plans -were under way for a number of "booster" stations throughout Canada to make it possible for programs to be well received from coast to coast. Something along this line appears to be
[Mr. Bradette.l
very desirable, indeed imperative, but the first consideration would yet seem to be the increase in power of Canadian stations so that they may have a real chance on the air.
There is a growing feeling among Canadian radio owners, and especially among the sufferers in the north, that not only do the people to the south believe that they won the war, but also that they rule the waves-the waves of the air. The winning of the war is a question that need not be debated at this time, but for the progress of the radio in Canada it seems surely necessary that Canada should rule her ow-n part of the air. There is little to be gained by discussion in the matter. Canada's rights are unassailable from a moral standpoint, but in a practical -way these rights are of no effect unless the dominion is in a position to enforce and uphold the rights that cannot be disputed but that are constantly disregarded. The only way to secure fair play is by the establishment of radio broadcast stations with power enough to take their place on the air against all comers. If Canada had one or two stations of 75,000 watt po-wer there would be little difficulty in the allotment of wave lengths as between this country and the one to the south. To the layman, and to the great majority of radio fans, it appears inevitable and inescapable that the first duty of the Canadian radio commission is to provide for one or more radio stations of such power that they will be able to take and hold their place on the air against all comers.
These are all the arguments that I want to put forward in this case. I have much confidence in the chairman of the radio commission, although I might state that at one time I did not entirely agree with him in regard to the trans-Canada highway, and through his newspaper I received a very cavalier answer, asking who I was, because I dared to question some of his statements on that question. Well, I am a Canadian, and a resident of northern Ontario and am proud of the fact. So with all respect to his wonderful qualifications- because I do not doubt them-I hope the present chairman of the radio commission will treat me as a Canadian and not as he treated me in his newspaper on that occasion. I might state that so far I have received satisfaction from the commission. I think Mr. Charlesworth knows northern Ontario, at any rate the mining sections; I believe he has visited that part of the province on several occasions. Therefore he should know our local conditions, and be able to deal with our problem. I believe he is animated by the true Canadian spirit, and will give the sparsely populated sections the same efficient service as the more populous ones. We in that northern area are doing a useful pioneer .work, binding the country together; where formerly there was a great unpopulated gap between east and west, in the last twenty years nearly 300,000 people have settled there. I hope the department and the radio commis-mission will find it possible to study on the
