ground the situation that exists so as to get first hand information.
I know the chairman must have a certain amount of qualification for his office or he would not be there. He is an art critic, a man who knows music and what music means to people, knows what a good musical program will mean to people in isolated sections. I hope the minister and the chairman of the radio commission will use all their influence so that in the near future our section will receive the attention it deserves. I express this hope because I am going to quote now certain words of the present chairman of the radio commission in an interview he gave to one of the writers for MacLean's Magazine. He wound up his interview in the following way:
Censorship, however, is not one of Mr Charleswor.th's chief interests. He is interested primarily in the upbuilding of a national system of broadcasting, the development of Canada's musicians and vocalists, in the providing of high class entertainment for radio listeners. Above all, he covets for this country success in that new field, the "theatre of the air."
Those are fine words, with which all Canadians will thoroughly agree. In my section particularly they were a message of hope, and we expect this department and the radio commission at the earliest possible moment to do away with the anomaly which at present exists and under which it is absolutely impossible to give our fine pioneer population the radio reception it deserves.

speechtext: Just a word in reply to my hon. friend. When the Aird commission

The minister has told us that that company has bought out the London Free Press station, no doubt at a stiff price, because in years gone by it was a profitable station. speechtext: Replying to the hon. gentleman's last question, it is not very long ago that I made a statement of the kind he refers to-about a month ago.
Longer than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: -and I have had no report since. I understood, when the recommendations came to me about the amalgamation of these two stations, that it would improve the situation in that respect. As regards the other question the hon. gentleman asks, as to whether stations that have acquired licences since the report of the Aird commission would get compensation in case of nationalization, I am not prepared to give a definite answer at the present time. We have made such reservation as will protect the national exchequer. They were all notified very clearly that, they could not expect compensation in the event of nationalization; they were accepting the licences and making their expenditures at their own risk. What the policy of the government would be in the event of the acquisition of any stations I am not prepared to say.
Would the minister say that the purchase of the London station by the Windsor station would justify the government in paying a higher price than the Windsor station would otherwise fetch?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I do not think it

Of course not. With regard to the Windsor station, it might have charged to its capital account what was paid for the London station although it has no actual assets to show for that payment. It was merely putting a competitor out of the way.

Windsor got the

And cancel them.

The minister still has n

What investigation has the minister made as to the wisdom of cancelling that licence?

Is London still operating?

subtopic: VANCOUVER, VICTORIA AND EASTERN-NORTHERN PACIFIC AGREEMENT
VANCOUVER, VICTORIA AND EASTERN-NORTHERN PACIFIC AGREEMENT
speechtext: This bill was before the railway committee and it passed through without any opposition. If I remember correctly, the Department of Railways and Canals said that they had no objection whatever to the passage of this measure, and it seems rather strange now to have the statement made to the house by the hon. member for Yale that the abandonment of the line is going to work a hardship on many people who have settled in that district. If such is the case I think the house ought to give serious consideration to the representations of the hon. member for the district, and perhaps allow the bill to stand if there is going to be any such hardship as he has indicated.

subtopic: VANCOUVER, VICTORIA AND EASTERN-NORTHERN PACIFIC AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Was the hon. member
in when I commenced my statement? I said at the beginning that with the merits of this particular bill and what it desired to do I was not concerned. This matter I have raised is the action of that same company in a different part of British Columbia. I chose this opportunity of placing the facts before the committee.

speakeroldname: The CHAIRMAN (Mr. Cowan, Port Arthur-Thunder Bay):
subtopic: VANCOUVER, VICTORIA AND EASTERN-NORTHERN PACIFIC AGREEMENT
speechtext: In the committee section 1 was amended, changing the date of the agreement from the first day of October, 1931, to the first day of November, 1932. Shall the section as amended be adopted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VANCOUVER, VICTORIA AND EASTERN-NORTHERN PACIFIC AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I have listened to the
observations of the hon. member for Yale and have been much impressed with the fact during the progress of the discussion on another measure that our law must be very much less useful than I thought it was with respect to matters of this kind. I confess my view was that a line could not be abandoned without the consent of the railway commission, but apparently that is not the law as it now reads. When in this country we charter a company to build a railway we authorize them within a given time to construct a line 
of rail of the standard width from one point to another. I say we charter them to do so within a given time, and by our standard form of charter we usually provide that if they do not complete that line to the point named within the time limit specified, the charter rights shall be forfeited with respect to that portion of the line which has not been completed.
It should follow that any line thus built under authority of a statute of this parliament could not be abandoned after people had settled beside it, without authority from some source beyond the mere management of the company itself. The argument in times past has been that railroads were profitable or they would not be built, and that therefore the necessity for having the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners was not apparent. I purpose suggesting to my colleagues the necessity of having an amendment made this session to the Railway Act to provide that no abandonment of a line may fake place without the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. I believe it is highly in the public interest that such provision should be made.
When the statement was made by the hon. member for Yale he was referring to a condition not dealt with by this bill, but to a condition in his own community which in principle was somewhat similar to the proposal dealt with by the agreement which this parliament is asked to ratify. And inasmuch as it involves a question of the abandonment of facilities which have been made available through permission granted by a law making authority, whether dt be that of the parliament of Canada or a legislature of a province, I believe we should pause and seriously consider the matter before we jeopardize the interests of those who in good faith -may have settled and made their homes, and have calculated upon the maintenance of a service to enable them to transport the products of their farms to markets, wherever they may be.
Under those circumstances I suggest that the hon. member in charge of the bill might move the committee up and ask for leave to sit again, in order that the Minister of Railways, who is absent, and the rest of the government may consider the matter more oarefully. I believe the case made out for the necessity of enacting general legislation has been such that it is the duty of the government, at the present session, to make a short amendment to the Railway Act.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Barber in the chair.
Radio service, to provide for the construction and maintenance of radio ship to shore stations and the general administration of the provisions of the Radio Act and regulations throughout the dominion, $679,550.
Carried.
No, it is not carried.

You are not through
broadcasting.

I should like to read from
a speech made by the Prime Minister on May 18 last year, as it appears at page 3036 of Hansard. Speaking of the licence fees and the moneys to be expended by the radio commission, he said:
We therefore in this measure for the present have provided that capital expenditures and all expenditures shall be within the income derived from the licence fees. That is, if there are 500,000 licences at $2 per licence, the commission would have an income of $1,000,000, which sum would not be more than expended by the commission in any one year.
The impression left upon the house at the time was that no money would be expended on radio broadcasting or any public service connected therewith, except that which was collected in licence fees. It now appears from the estimates for this year that the radio commission are asking permission to spend a million dollars on broadcasting, or whatever they are doing. But here is another item not charged to the radio commission. The sum of $280,400 for broadcasting improvement is charged to a department of government. That is to say, the commission being held down to an agreed sum, that is, not being allowed to spend any more than the licence fees, other expenditures which it is desired to make in connection with the same service can be made by a department of government. It seems to me that is breaking the spirit, if not the letter, of the act.
Let us see what the position is. Before the radio commission was set up the licence fee was only one dollar. AH of that dollar went into the public treasury. Out of the amount, which went into the public revenue the sum-of $280,400 was taken out for certain services"-in connection with radio, as outlined in item 140. The balance of the fees, something like-half a million dollars, was left in the public-treasury to ease the burdens of the taxpayers. The licence fee has now been doubled. Two dollars goes into the treasury, and all of it is turned over to the radio commission. In addition to that, $280,400 can be taken out of the treasury to do the work that was being paid for by the licences. The result is that whatever the revenue from the dollar licence amounted to, if as the Prime Minister says there are 770,000 radios in this country it means that $770,000 that would have been paid into the treasury and made available for this public service is now diverted to radio and therefore has to be replaced out of the pockets of the taxpayers. So I say that this method of doing things is actually taking out of the pockets of the people some $700,000, and breaking the letter if not the spirit of the act.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I gladly avail myself of this opportunity to make a statement with respect to the policy of the government in connection with radio broadcasting. This house unanimously decided-
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This house unanimously decided-
No, I voted against it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may have expressed his disagreement, but that only tends to show how great the unanimity was. This house, with a single exception then, expressed its view that radio broadcasting in Canada should be a public utility. A commission investigated the matter at some length. The commission made a report. The report was unanimous. It was adopted by the House
Supply-Marine-Radio

of Commons. The hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Young) says he was opposed to it; I recall that he was. A bill giving effect to the recommendation was introduced. It passed this house without division. That bill provided that radio service in Canada should be a publicly owned utility. A contract was made by the parliament of Canada by statute with radio users in Canada that the $2 licence fee collected from them should be used for the purpose of providing them with radio service. There is therefore outstanding in Canada today a contract by which this parliament undertook that we would collect from licensees at the rate of S2 per licence certain sums of money to be held in trust and utilized for the purpose of radio broadcasting, supplying radio service. Now, the attacks that have been made are being made for the purpose of destroying this publicly owned service.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The people who are desirous of destroying it are not numerous, but they are very vocal, and their influence is painfully apparent in many places. The effect upon other countries on this continent of establishing in this country publicly owned radio service will be very great. The opposition to our system is not limited to Canada. Those who are assisting in the opposition to the public ownership of this service are aiding and abetting the private ownership of what in my judgment cannot, in a new country, with the great extensions of knowledge being made from year to year, be properly committed to a private interest.
The money about which the hon. member for Weyburn speaks is therefore money collected from licensees for the purpose of providing radio service. Under our constitution that money is paid into the consolidated revenue fund, but it is earmarked as a trust fund for the purpose mentioned in the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932. The duty of the government is to make available to that commission the money that is collected for the purpose mentioned in the statute. To do that an estimate has to be submitted to this parliament. In a sense it is a pro forma estimate, for under the statute of last year it is money in trust for the development of the radio service; not to be used for any purpose you may please, but to be used for just one purpose, the providing of radio service for the Canadian people. Unfortunately-and the government must take the responsibility for it-when the estimate was printed it was not made clear that this was merely releasing to the commission the money thus collected.

Had it stated, as it should have stated, and I must assum/e the responsibility for its not being done, that this money was merely being released for the purposes for which parliament had declared it should be used, there never would have been any difficulty about it.
Does that apply to this item of $280,400?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am coming to that. There has gone throughout the country a statement that the Canadian people in these days of grim adversity are voting a million dollars for radio. That is not correct. What has happened is that a limited number of Canadians have provided at the rate of $2 per licence a sum much in excess of a million dollars-to be exact, up to the moment $1,400,000-for this sendee. A million dollars of it is contained in that item, and I think the criticism of the hon. member for Wey-bum, that it is not clear that the balance necessary to maintain that service should come from this amount, has not been established. Nevertheless that money that is necessary, whatever sum, is for two purposes; first, to provide a service-I propose to have submitted to this house next week a resolution providing for the purchase by the radio commission of the Canadian National Railways radio plant. The plant is being bought for the sum of $50,000, if I remember aright. Of course it cost a good deal more than that, but as it was a branch of a government owned railway the railway officials expressed the view that it should be placed in the hands of the commission. The engineers agreed upon the price, but as the statute says this purchase could be made only with the approval of parliament, it is proposed that a resolution shall be presented to this house and to the Senate of Canada in order that parliament may express its approval of the purchase of these facilities for the sum I have mentioned.
This item, in the words in which it now stands, is to provide for the improvement of reception service, doing away with interference in connection therewith. In my judgment that sum will have to be deducted from the licence fees that are paid into the consolidated revenue fund, because it is a part of the maintenance of the service.
That is good.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The other item, as the hon. gentleman properly points out, has reference to the maintenance of our safety radio stations on the coast lines of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It involves a large sum of money. Once more it is the old story: when

Supply-Marine-Radio
some newspaper editor, with a wider knowledge of Canadian conditions than members of this parliament or this government, undertakes to expose the wasteful use of public moneys in connection with radio, he is talking about something with respect to which he knows absolutely nothing; for as I have tried to make clear to this house,-and every hon. gentleman can take the statute and look at it for himself,-the money is money paid under a trust for providing radio for the Canadian people.
There is another item, dealing with ship to shore stations and direction finding and the safety of life and ships coming into our ports. Why are we spending this money? Well, Canada must do one of two things: either expect marine insurance rates to be doubled, or maintain radio stations for the purpose of enabling ships to determine their position by radio and to maintain in fog and storm constant communication between ship and shore and ship and ship in order that there may be safety for all who go down to the sea in ships, passengers and crew.
There are a number of such items. This affords one an opportunity to say that, owing to the fact that we have long coast lines, we are compelled to spend literally millions of dollars in bearing our share of the international obligations that rest upon all maritime peoples; to maintain light service, buoys, aids to navigation, direction finding stations, fog horns, everything that goes to make for safety of ships, alike for passengers and crews. When one reads ill-considered statements as to why we should pare down this or that estimate I can only say that I could go through our estimates and show how little really is under the control of any government in these times, how slight is our control with respect to these items. I received a letter yesterday, I think, asking why the members of parliament do not cut down their indemnities by SI,000 and why the cabinet ministers do not cut down their stipends by $3,000 or $4,000. Every service is to be cut except the service in which the individual is directly interested; there must be no cut in that. I am not going to do more than say that if you take these estimates and ask yourselves on what one item you could expend less money than this government is asking for, all you have to do to answer the question is to investigate the character of the service rendered.
So far as this particular item is concerned the Canadian people have made a choice between the privately owned and the publicly owned enterprise. Having concluded that we are going to own our own radio service we
must have patience to see that, in the face of great difficulty and opposition, and a very earnest desire on the part of those opposed to the principle to destroy it before it is well bom, it gets a fair chance. A fair chance means that the money which a limited number of the Canadian people have paid for radio service, which money is paid into the consolidated revenues of the country earmarked as a trust fund for a particular purpose, which we must vote in order to release it and make it available for that purpose, shall be used so that every encouragement is given the enterprise which we brought into being unanimously-pardon me, with a single exception, the hon. member for Weybum-so that it may grow up and become a real, virile Canadian industry.

I am quite satisfied with the explanation given with regard to the item for $679,000; it is quite reasonable. I am also glad to know that this item of $280,400 is to be charged against the funds available to the commission and made up of the licence fees collected. There is one statement, however, in connection with which I should like a little further information. I understood the Prime Minister to say that there was a contract between the government of Canada, or the radio commission, and the licence holders, and that it was a part of that contract that the licence fee should be $2. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, I said the fee was
fixed at S2. The hon. gentleman will remember that it was so stated by the minister last year when his estimates were under consideration. The contract is that the money derived from licence fees should be utilized for the purpose of providing a radio service in .accordance with the terms of the act passed last session. In my judgment that is a statutory trust between this parliament and those who pay their money for licences.
There is no assurance that the licence fee will not be varied from time to time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, I think that is a
matter of regulation.

I should like to ask the
minister if he has taken up with the commission the idea of broadcasting to ships on the Atlantic coast, in the way broadcasting is being carried on in the west. At the present time there is a service on the Pacific coast by means of which all ships are in constant touch with the radio stations, from which they get the news of the day while at sea. I understand that this service is greatly appre-
Supply-M arine*-Radio

ciated, and I should like to know whether steps have been taken to provide a similar service on the Atlantic coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I may tell my hon. friend that consideration is presently being given to the introduction of a similar service on the Atlantic coast.

Having
regard to the announcement just made by the Prime Minister that the commission will take over the Canadian National broadcasting service I should like to ask if any policy has been formulated as yet with regard to broadcasting in the maritime provinces. I may tell the minister that the station at Moncton owned by the Canadian National is obsolete, and I hope the commission are not paying very much for it. I think the people down there are anxious to have a national station established in that community as soon as possible, and if any policy has been adopted I should like to know what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I know that the radio commission is working at present on the location of stations all over Canada in order to satisfy every part of the dominion. Of course their work has not been completed, but I know they are endeavouring to select the best possible location in order to satisfy the Canadian people.

In connection with these
range finding stations I may say that one was established in the district I represent some six or seven years ago, and it has done excellent work. I rather think another was established recently, but one plant has been in operation for several years. It is located along a section of the coast that was formerly known as the graveyard of the Pacific, and that name was fully justified. I walked along that coast a number of years ago, and at least once in every mile, and sometimes oftener, there would be the wreck of a boat lying on the beach. I would ask what that was, and I would be told that it was such and such a boat that went ashore several years before. So far as I know, and I think I am in a position to speak with certainty, since the establishment of that range finding station there has not been a single considerable wreck on the west coast of Vancouver island. The cost of the station has been amply repaid, not only in the saving of lives but also in the saving of ships and property.

I should like to ask the minister if any definite policy has been laid down in connection with the collection of licence fees. A week or two

ago, when this item was up for discussion, I told the committee the difficulty experienced by myself and the others in parts of my constituency in finding anyone who would take the money for radio licence fees.
The postmaster.

I know some people never paid their licence fees because they could not find anyone who would take it. I inquired at the post offices, the town halls and the radio dealers in two towns in my constituency and was unable to find the proper person. I have had letters this year asking how to get a licence, because no notice has been given, and I do not know the answer myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There has been no change in the system of collecting fees; the postmasters, the radio dealers and some banks are authorized to sell licences. The only change is that we have authorized the supervisors, who were appointed last year, to canvass from house to house after April 1, and they receive the same commission that is paid the banks or the dealers, which is 15 cents per licence. If there is any locality which is not provided with a vendor of licences I should be glad to be notified and the matter will be attended to immediately. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The matter has been considered from every angle. In Great Britain the post office looks after the interference with individual reception and the broadcasting corporation looks after matters connected 53719-264
with the facilities of the corporation. The matter is being considered; whatever experience teaches us is in the public interest will be done. I saw Mr. Gladstone Murray the other day for the purpose of ascertaining just how it had worked out in England, and the minister and I have been discussing the matter at some length in the light of the knowledge we have obtained. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was not in his place when I explained the matter; if he had been here he would have heard the whole explanation. This is an item that appeared in previous years with respect to the improvement of reception by individual licence holders. Item 247, to which attention has been directed, deals directly with the operations of the broadcasting commission itself. I wonder if the Prime Minister would permit me another question in order to clear up the matter. Is that amount of $284,000 paid under the Radio Act or under the radio broadcasting act? In fairness to the

Only in the unorganized districts?

Where there are no

They receive the

speechtext: Generally the licences are purchased from a dealer, a post office or a bank, but the opportunity to canvass for licences has been given to men who are out of work.

I do not want to delay
these estimates but I object to the way in which radio licence fees are collected. It seems to be a haphazard system. As citizens we have understood that if we had a radio receiving set we would have to go to that post office to secure our licence. This was a similar provision to that prevailing in Ontario in the case of motor car licences. However, if we operate a motor car without a licence no one comes around to canvass us and coax us to buy one, we are prosecuted for operating a car without a licence. If the minister proposes to sell licences only through these canvassers, well and good, but I do not think he should continue the present system as well. What do these men do when they go to a house and find that a radio set has been operated for five years? Do they ask to see the licences for the back years? the improvement of radio reception. Is this bad reception due to some policy of the new radio broadcasting commission, or can it be corrected by the minister's department under this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I am informed that this trouble is due to power lines in and around Ottawa. We have that trouble in many parts of the country, and we are trying to improve the situation as much as possible.
It is a strange thing that the power line trouble should have started just after the radio commission got functioning.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There may be something in the way of changing wave lengths also. It is an experiment, it is temporary; they try a certain wave length for certain stations; it may be changed later on in order to improve the reception. I understand that the radio commission is trying to find the best means of doing away with this interference.

I do not want to labour the point, but there is a great deal in what the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pou-liot) said. There was none of this trouble when Commander Edwards had full charge of the situation in Canada. If Commander Edwards has to look after radio reception and improving the service for listeners it seems very strange that there should be this fooling with and changing wave lengths that almost wrecks the reception in the capital from most stations that the people have been listening to in the past. The minister must see the articles in the papers; there was a long one in this evening's Journal. They are becoming very common. The minister would be well advised to put both radio broadcasting and radio reception under the command of someone who is technically expert and able to look after it. He has in his department an officer who is said to be one of the best radio men on this continent, and it seems to me unpardonable that when the commission begins operation, reception should be spoiled through the changing of wave lengths, making it utterly impossible for the department under this vote to correct it. Money is being spent to improve reception, and on the other hand the commission is changing wave lengths and ruining reception. It is really serious, and I think the minister should look into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: This appropriation is for the purpose of maintaining in good condition the dams constructed in the years 1929 to 1931 in the St. Lawrence river below Sorel, to retard the flow of the river and thereby maintain a higher level, including Montreal harbour. Some repairs had to be made to these dams. The water made some encroachments on the banks, and repairs had to be made, and will have to be made. It is an absolutely necessary expenditure.
Where are the dams?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: In the Sorel islands.
Can tlfe minister give any information as to what has been the result of building these dams?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
According to Sir
Alexander Gibb's report, these dams have increased the depth of the water at Sorel by a foot and a few inches, and at Montreal by five inches.
Has the department received any complaints that because of these dams the flow of water is more rapid in the main channel than it was previously, and therefore more dangerous?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It has increased the current a little,-but not to a great extent.
Has the department any information in regard to the flow to-day as compared with that of the time prior to the construction of the dams?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think we have that at the office. But I know from the report of Sir Alexander Gibb that the velocity of the current at the present time is still reasonable. It is not dangerous to navigation.

Can the minister give the committee any information with regard to the condition of these dams to-day as compared with when they were first put in? Is it not true that these dams are made of rock

Last year little
breaches were made, but not much. The damage from the water was on the banks. Of course there is settlement of the dams. It takes perhaps two or three years before they are absolutely settled.

Could the minister give any information in regard to the depth of the top of these dams or dykes below the surface of the water? That is, what amount of water flows over the top of them at the average flow? Do these dams come right up to the top?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Not exactly. *
How far down are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have not a definite statement, but I kn-ow they do not come up to the water level.
How many of these dams have we at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

Where are they located?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: All in the Sorel islands below Sorel.
Is there just one main channel left without any dams at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, two. There is only one main channel, the ship channel; there is another channel on the north side of the river.

speechtext: I know that the English public relations man is paid $5,800 less ten per cent, so that the other must get the difference.

Why was it necessary to pay such a salary to the publicity man?
I understand there are publicity men in the other departments, the Trade and Commerce department, for instance. My information is that the publicity man in the Department of Trade and Commerce does not get nearly so large a salary. Why a publicity man in broadcasting? What does he do? Does he talk over the radio? Is that his function, business or duty? In short, precisely what does he do?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am told he is a
very useful man in >the publication of programs and in publicity in connection with the [DOT] operations of the commission. The position is not a new one; it exists in other countries. He has to get in touch with all the newspapers in Canada, because listeners like to be informed by the newspapers as to what programs are being broadcast. Is he sober all the time?

I do not think the
minister has made it very clear how this publicity man will earn his salary of $5,800 a year. I have always been under the impression that the chairman of the commission was the man who arranged -the programs. Somebody said he was a music critic, having followed that line for some years in the newspaper business. Why there should be a publicity man at $5,800 a year I cannot understand. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The salary was fixed by order in council and we came to the conclusion that $5,800 less ten per cent was a fair remuneration for the position.

I agree with the minister that it is a fairly good salary these days, $5,800. In the selection of the staff, or in the arrangement as to what they were to be paid, was the minister consulted by the chairman of the commission? That raises the whole point again. It does appear to me that there is overlapping between the department under the minister and the commission under the chairman, and while we have endeavoured, not once but many times, to get from the minister some information as to who really is in charge, we have not succeeded. Is he over the chairman or is the chairman over him, or do they work together? There must be one head. If there is any conflict between the minister and the chairman of the commission there is bound to be trouble all the time. I would not like to think that the chairman was over the minister. I feel that a minister of the crown should have absolute control over a public servant. No matter how eminent a man this chairman may be, no matter what he did before he got into this work, he is a public servant and should be responsible to the minister who in turn is responsible to parliament for everything done in connection with the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: As I told the committee this afternoon, the act gives full powers to the commission in connection with the allocation of stations, the power of stations, wave lengths and so on. I do not think it is the duty of the minister to interfere with the commission in that respect.

Subject always to the approval of the minister. This afternoon the minister said that he had issued instructions to the commission, I think in connection with the Windsor station. If he issued instructions to the commission, he must consider that he 
has control over the commission and that they are responsible to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There must be a misunderstanding about that statement in connection with the Windsor station; I did not issue instructions.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I may have expressed the desire that they do so but I cannot give any orders where the act gives them absolute powers.
It is a very humiliating position for a minister not to have control over a commission which is practically in his department and which spends a vast amount of money.
